qs.q: Which OS service is provided by a command-line interpreter or a graphical desktop?

c.x: Resource allocation
User interface
Error detection
Logging

qs.e: The user interface service lets users interact with the OS through a graphical user interface (GUI) or a command-line interface (CLI). User interface = GUI or CLI

qs.q: Which statement correctly describes the program execution service?

c.x: The OS loads programs into memory and runs them, and a program may end normally or abnormally
The OS loads programs into memory and runs them, but a program can end only normally
The OS runs programs directly from disk without loading them, and ends them abnormally only
The OS loads programs into memory but leaves the running of them to the user process

qs.e: The program execution service must load a program into memory and run it, and the program must be able to end its execution either normally or abnormally. <mark>Load, run, end (normally or abnormally)</mark>

qs.q: Why must the OS provide processes with some means to perform I/O?

c.x: Because I/O devices can be used only during the boot process
Because user processes can perform I/O only on files, not on devices
Because user processes cannot execute I/O operations directly
Because I/O operations are executed only by the user interface service

qs.e: User processes cannot execute I/O operations directly, so the OS provides the I/O operations service as the means through which they perform I/O. <mark>No direct I/O for user processes</mark>

qs.q: A text editor saves a document to disk and later deletes an old backup file. Which OS service does it rely on?

c.x: Communications
Error detection
Resource allocation
File-system manipulation

qs.e: Reading, writing, creating and deleting files are the operations offered by the file-system manipulation service. File-system manipulation

qs.q: Two processes need to exchange information. Which pair lists the two ways the OS can implement this communications service?

c.x: Message passing or file locking
Shared memory or message passing
Shared memory or device drivers
Message passing or program loading

qs.e: The communications service lets user processes exchange information, and it is implemented via shared memory or message passing. Shared memory or message passing

qs.q: What is the purpose of the error detection service?

c.x: To record which process uses how much of each kind of resource
To allocate processor time and memory to every running process
To ensure correct computing by detecting hardware and program errors
To control all access to the resources of the whole system

qs.e: Error detection ensures correct computing by detecting errors in the hardware or in user programs. The other options describe logging, resource allocation and protection. <mark>Detect hardware and program errors</mark>

qs.q: A company bills each department according to how much and what kinds of resources its processes used. Which OS function supplies the data needed for billing?

c.x: Logging
Protection
Resource allocation
Error detection

qs.e: Logging records which process uses how much and what kinds of resources; this record may be used for account billing or for accumulating usage statistics. Logging

qs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes protection from security?

c.x: Protection records resource usage, while security allocates resources to processes
Protection defends against outsiders, while security controls all access to resources
Protection detects hardware errors, while security detects errors in user programs
Protection controls all access to resources, while security defends against outsiders

qs.e: Protection ensures that all access to system resources is controlled, whereas security concerns defending the system from outsiders. <mark>Protection = controlled access; security = defence from outsiders</mark>

qs.q: Which additional OS function gives resources such as CPU time and memory to the running processes?

c.x: Logging
Resource allocation
Protection
Communications

qs.e: Resource allocation is the function that allocates resources to the running processes. Resource allocation

qs.q: What is a system call?

c.x: A function that lets the OS call user processes directly
A hardware instruction that lets programs bypass the kernel
An interface through which user processes request OS services
A command typed in the CLI to start a new program

qs.e: System calls provide an interface to the services of the OS; user processes use them to call those services. <mark>System call = interface to OS services</mark>

qs.q: Which statement about how system calls are made available to programmers is correct?

c.x: They are C and C++ functions, and some low-level tasks may use assembly language
They are written only in assembly language, so C and C++ cannot invoke them
They are C and C++ functions, and assembly language is never used for them
They are available only through the GUI, with no functions for programmers

qs.e: System calls are available as functions written in C and C++, while some low-level tasks may be written in assembly language. <mark>C and C++ functions, plus assembly for low-level tasks</mark>

qs.q: What happens when a process executes a system call?

c.x: The process switches itself to kernel mode and runs the service on its own
The OS terminates the process and restarts it once the service finishes
The CPU skips the OS and runs the service while staying in user mode
The system traps to the OS, which then performs the requested service

qs.e: When a process executes a system call, the system traps to the OS, which carries out the requested service. Trap to the OS

qs.q: What does API stand for, and what is it used for?

c.x: Application Process Interface, used to schedule the processes of the system
Application Programming Interface, used by programmers to invoke OS services
Automatic Programming Interface, used to compile programs written in C and C++
Application Program Instruction, used to load the kernel into memory at boot

qs.e: API stands for Application Programming Interface; the OS provides it to application programmers to invoke its services. <mark>API = Application Programming Interface</mark>

qs.q: In the lecture's `open()` example, the system call interface uses the index i to look up the System Call Table. What does the table entry provide?

c.x: The parameters that the user application passed to `open()`
The value that is finally returned to the user application
A pointer to the implementation of the system call in the kernel
The code of the user application that called `open()`

qs.e: The system call interface uses the index i to find the entry in the System Call Table, and that entry holds a pointer to the implementation of `open()` inside the kernel. Table entry = pointer to the implementation

qs.q: Which sequence correctly describes how a call to `open()` is handled in the lecture's example?

c.x: Application → system call interface → System Call Table → implementation in kernel mode → return to the application
Application → System Call Table → system call interface → implementation in kernel mode → return to the application
Application → implementation in kernel mode → System Call Table → system call interface → return to the application
Application → system call interface → implementation in kernel mode → System Call Table → return to the application

e: The user application, running in user mode, calls `open()`.
The call enters the system call interface, which uses the index i to look in the System Call Table.
The table entry points to the implementation of `open()` in kernel mode, which runs and then returns.
The result goes back through the system call interface to the user application.

qs.q: In the lecture's `open()` example, in which mode does each part run?

c.x: Application in kernel mode; implementation in user mode
Application and implementation both in user mode
Application and implementation both in kernel mode
Application in user mode; implementation in kernel mode

qs.e: The user application runs in user mode, while the System Call Table and the implementation of `open()` are in kernel mode. User mode → kernel mode

qs.q: In the lecture's Method 2 example for passing parameters, what does the user program load into a CPU register before executing `system call 13`?

c.x: The parameters themselves, one value in each register
The address X of the block that stores the parameters
The size of the parameter table X in memory
A pointer to the code for system call 13 in the OS

qs.e: In Method 2 the parameters are stored in a table (block) in memory, and only the address X of that block is passed in a CPU register. Register holds the address of the block

qs.q: How does the stack method pass parameters to the OS?

c.x: The OS pushes them onto the stack, and the process pops them off later
The process stores them in a memory table and passes its address in a register
The process pushes them onto the stack, and the OS pops them off later
The process loads them directly into CPU registers before the system call

qs.e: In Method 3 the process pushes the parameters onto the stack and the operating system later pops them off. <mark>Process pushes, OS pops</mark>

qs.q: Which option correctly matches the three methods of passing parameters to system calls?

c.x: 1: CPU registers; 2: memory block whose address is in a register; 3: stack
1: stack; 2: CPU registers; 3: memory block whose address is in a register
1: memory block whose address is in a register; 2: stack; 3: CPU registers
1: CPU registers; 2: stack; 3: memory block whose address is in a register

qs.e: Method 1 passes the parameters in CPU registers, Method 2 stores them in a memory block and passes its address in a register, and Method 3 uses the stack. <mark>1: registers, 2: memory block, 3: stack</mark>

qs.q: In the Method 2 example, the user program has loaded the address X into a register and then executes `system call 13`. How does the OS get the parameters?

c.x: It pops the parameters off the stack that the process prepared
It reads the parameters directly from the CPU registers
It receives the parameters in a message from the user program
It reads address X from the register and uses the parameters in table X

e: The user program stores the parameters in table X in memory and loads the address X into a register.
The OS code for system call 13 reads the address X from the register.
It then uses the parameters stored in table X.
<mark>Register gives the address; the parameters are read from table X</mark>

qs.q: Which type of system call includes wait event, signal event, and allocate and free memory?

c.x: File management
Process control
Device management
Information maintenance

qs.e: Process control covers creating, loading, executing, terminating and aborting processes, plus waiting for time or events, signaling events and allocating or freeing memory. Process control

qs.q: A program asks the OS to reposition within a file and then close it. Which type of system call is it using?

c.x: Device management
Information maintenance
File management
Communications

qs.e: Opening, closing, reading, writing and repositioning a file are file management system calls. File management

qs.q: A process asks for exclusive use of a device and later gives it back. Which type of system call is this?

c.x: Device management
File management
Process control
Communications

qs.e: Requesting a device and releasing it are device management system calls. Device management

qs.q: Which type of system call includes get time/date and set time/date?

c.x: Process control
Device management
Communications
Information maintenance

qs.e: Getting and setting the time/date or system data are information maintenance system calls. Information maintenance

qs.q: Which of the following is <u>not</u> a communications system call?

c.x: Send message
Reposition file
Transfer status information
Attach remote device

qs.e: Sending messages, transferring status information and attaching remote devices are communications calls, while repositioning a file belongs to file management. Reposition file is not a communications call

qs.q: What is a system boot?

c.x: The process of installing the kernel onto the root file system
The process of copying user programs from disk into memory
The process of starting a computer by loading the kernel
The process of restarting the kernel after a system call fails

qs.e: System boot is the process of starting a computer by loading the kernel. <mark>Boot = starting the computer by loading the kernel</mark>

qs.q: Which sequence correctly lists the steps of the boot process on most systems?

c.x: Locate the kernel → load and start it → initialize hardware → mount the root file system
Load and start the kernel → locate it → initialize hardware → mount the root file system
Locate the kernel → load and start it → mount the root file system → initialize hardware
Initialize hardware → locate the kernel → load and start it → mount the root file system

e: The kernel is loaded into memory and started.
<mark>Locate → load and start → initialize hardware → mount root file system</mark>

qs.q: Which statement about the boot process is correct?

c.x: The kernel locates itself, and then the bootstrap program initializes the hardware
The bootstrap program mounts the root file system before the kernel is loaded
The kernel is loaded into memory only after the root file system is mounted
The bootstrap program locates the kernel, and then the kernel initializes the hardware

qs.e: The bootstrap program is responsible for locating the kernel; once the kernel is loaded and started, it initializes the hardware, and the root file system is mounted afterwards. <mark>Bootstrap locates; kernel initializes hardware</mark>

qs.q: Which statement describes the monolithic approach?

c.x: The kernel is divided into layers, and each layer uses only the lower layers
The kernel is a single static binary that runs in a single address space
The kernel keeps only core functions, and services run as system programs
The kernel links additional services in as LKMs at boot or run time

qs.e: A monolithic kernel has no internal structure: it is a single, static binary file running in a single address space. The other options describe the layered, micro-kernel and modules approaches. <mark>Single static binary in one address space</mark>

qs.q: Why is communication inside a monolithic kernel fast, with very little system-call overhead?

c.x: Because every service runs as a separate user process and uses message passing
Because each layer calls only the layer directly beneath it in the structure
Because all kernel functionality is in one binary in a single address space
Because services are loaded dynamically only when they are actually needed

qs.e: Everything is in one binary running in a single address space, so kernel parts communicate quickly and the system-call interface adds very little overhead. The price is tight coupling, which makes the kernel hard to extend. <mark>One binary, one address space = fast</mark>

qs.q: Which statement about the layered approach is correct?

c.x: It is loosely coupled, because changes in one layer do not affect the others
It is tightly coupled, because changes in one layer affect all of the others
It is loosely coupled, because every layer may call every other layer directly
It is tightly coupled, because it is a single binary in a single address space

qs.e: The layered approach divides the OS into layers and is loosely coupled: a change in one layer does not affect the others. Tight coupling describes the monolithic approach. <mark>Layered = loosely coupled</mark>

qs.q: Why is it difficult to define the functionality of each layer in the layered approach?

c.x: Because every layer must be able to call every other layer directly
Because the layers are loaded and removed dynamically at run time as LKMs
Because every layer runs as a separate user process and uses message passing
Because each layer may use the functions of only the lower-level layers

qs.e: Since a layer can use only the functions of the layers below it, the functionality has to be assigned very carefully to the right layer, which makes defining each layer difficult. <mark>Lower layers only → hard to define layers</mark>

qs.q: In a layered OS, a service call has to pass through several layers. What is the result?

c.x: Better performance, because each layer adds optimizations
Poor performance, because many layers must be traversed
Tighter coupling, because the layers become dependent
Less flexibility, because the kernel becomes one binary

qs.e: Traversing multiple layers to call services results in poor performance. <mark>Many layers → poor performance</mark>

qs.q: In the lecture's micro-kernel diagram, which components are inside the microkernel running in kernel mode?

c.x: File system, device driver, and interprocess communication
Application program, file system, and memory management
Interprocess communication, memory management, and CPU scheduling
Application program, device driver, and CPU scheduling

qs.e: The microkernel keeps only interprocess communication, memory management and CPU scheduling. The application program, file system and device driver run in user mode. <mark>IPC, memory management, CPU scheduling</mark>

qs.q: In a micro-kernel system, how do the application program, file system, and device driver communicate?

c.x: By exchanging messages between the user-mode components
By calling each other directly inside a single address space
By sharing one System Call Table located in the kernel
By loading one another as LKMs while the system runs

qs.e: In the diagram, the user-mode components (application program, file system, device driver) communicate by messages. Message passing

qs.q: Why does the micro-kernel approach provide more security and reliability?

c.x: Because all services run in kernel mode, where the kernel can protect them
Because the kernel is one static binary that is hard to modify or attack
Because each layer can use only the functions of the lower-level layers
Because most services run as user processes, so one failing leaves the rest intact

qs.e: Most services run as user rather than kernel processes, so if a service fails, the rest of the operating system remains untouched. <mark>User-mode services isolate failures</mark>

qs.q: What is the modules approach to OS structure?

c.x: The kernel keeps only core functions, and everything else runs in user mode
The kernel has core components and can link in extra services via LKMs
The kernel is split into layers that may call only the layers below them
The kernel is one binary with no structure that runs in one address space

qs.e: The kernel has a set of core components and links in additional services via LKMs (Loadable Kernel Modules), at boot time or during run time, which is preferable to recompiling the kernel after every change. <mark>Core components + LKMs</mark>

qs.q: How does the modules approach differ from the micro-kernel approach?

c.x: Modules must use message passing, while micro-kernel services call each other directly
Modules run in user mode, while micro-kernel services run in kernel mode
Modules do not need message passing to communicate, unlike micro-kernel services
Modules keep only core functions, while micro-kernel services include everything

qs.e: Both approaches keep only core functions in the primary module, but modules do not need message passing to communicate. <mark>Modules communicate without message passing</mark>

qs.q: Compared with the layered approach, why is the modules approach more flexible?

c.x: Because any module can call any other module directly
Because each module may call only the modules below it
Because modules have no defined interface to protect them
Because the whole kernel is recompiled after every change

qs.e: Like the layered approach, each kernel section has a defined and protected interface, but any module can call any other module, which makes the design more flexible. <mark>Any module can call any other module</mark>

qs.q: Linux is described as both monolithic and modular. What is the reason for each?

c.x: Monolithic to add functionality dynamically; modular for efficient performance
Monolithic for strict layering; modular for message passing between services
Monolithic for better security; modular for easier porting to new hardware
Monolithic for efficient performance; modular to add functionality dynamically

qs.e: Linux is monolithic to provide very efficient performance and modular to add new functionality to the kernel dynamically, which is an example of a hybrid OS. Monolithic = performance; modular = dynamic functionality
